definition: Done secretly or quietly so that other people will not notice.
example: During the long speech, she stole a surreptitious glance at the clock.
nuance: Surreptitious stresses quietly avoiding notice; furtive adds a nervous, guilty air, and clandestine suggests an organized secret plan.
prompt: A hungry student wants a snack during a silent study hour in the school library.
options: Mia took a surreptitious bite of her granola bar while the librarian's back was turned.
Mia crunched her chips so loudly that her surreptitious snack drew stares from every table.
Feeling surreptitious, Mia knocked twice on the wooden table for luck before eating.
Mia stood on a chair and made a surreptitious announcement that snacks were now allowed.
reasons: Waiting until no one is watching to eat is exactly the kind of hidden act the word describes.
A snack that makes everyone stare is the opposite of one kept out of sight.
Knocking on wood for luck is superstitious, a look-alike word with a different meaning.
Standing up and announcing something to the room is open and public, not secret.

practice.prompt: A soccer team is planning a surprise party for its coach.
options: The coach was surreptitious of the cake, so she refused to try a single slice.
The party was surreptitious because it was the biggest one the team had ever thrown.
The players kept their surreptitious planning to whispered talks after practice.
The players' surreptitious plan was painted on a giant banner in the gym lobby.
reasons: This confuses the word with suspicious; being distrustful is not acting in secret.
A party's size says nothing about whether it was kept hidden.
Whispering out of the coach's hearing keeps the plan hidden, which fits the word.
A banner anyone can read gives the secret away instead of keeping it.
